quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Interests, BATNA, and Preparation
quizzes.intro: Check foundations before tactics, workplace scripts, and ethics deep dives.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a position and an interest?

options.text: They mean the same thing
A position is a stated demand; an interest is the underlying why
Interests are always dollar amounts only
Positions are illegal in workplace talks

questions.explanation: Interests unlock options when positions deadlock.

wrongExplanations.c: Interests include stability, recognition, speed, risk, and more.
wrongExplanations.d: Positions are normal; rigidity without interests is the problem.

options.text: A bluff you invent with no plan
Your best alternative if no agreement is reached
Your opening joke
A mandatory first concession

questions.explanation: BATNA reality creates calm leverage; fabricated walk-aways collapse.

wrongExplanations.a: Fake alternatives damage trust and fail under pressure.
wrongExplanations.c: Rapport helps but is not BATNA.

questions.prompt: Why separate target and reservation points?

options.text: So you can negotiate toward a target while protecting a walk-away line
Because only one number should exist in your mind
So you accept anything under social pressure
Because reservation points replace preparation

questions.explanation: Targets stretch outcomes; reservations prevent harmful deals.

wrongExplanations.c: Reservation exists to resist harmful pressure.
wrongExplanations.d: Preparation still includes interests, questions, and trades.

questions.prompt: What should a preparation checklist include?

options.text: Only hoping charm will suffice
Interests, BATNA, target/reservation, opening ask, trades, and questions
A plan to lie about alternatives
No written notes ever

wrongExplanations.a: Charm without prep is still unprepared.
wrongExplanations.d: Writing prep improves clarity and calm.

options.text: An absurd number with no rationale meant only to shock
An ambitious yet justified opening supported by data or scope facts
Your reservation stated first every time
Silence with no offer forever

questions.explanation: Anchors influence the zone when they are ambitious and credible.

wrongExplanations.c: Leading with reservation often leaves value.
wrongExplanations.d: Offers are part of negotiation; silence is a tactic, not a substitute for all anchors.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Offers, Concessions, and Workplace Deals
quizzes.intro: Test packages, concessions, salary/scope talks, and process discipline.

questions.prompt: Why use package offers when multiple issues exist?

options.text: They reveal trade-offs and reduce deadlock on a single variable
They hide all terms forever
They ban questions
They require burning the relationship

questions.explanation: Packages let parties trade across differently valued issues.

options.text: Spill large unilateral discounts quickly under silence
Plan, pace, and trade concessions for something in return
Never move under any circumstances
Concede first on your reservation without a target

questions.explanation: Planned traded concessions teach counterparts you will not fold for free.

wrongExplanations.a: Rapid unilateral concessions invite waiting you out.
wrongExplanations.c: Some movement is often needed for deals.

questions.prompt: What is a strong response to an impossible scope/date ask?

options.text: Silent despair until failure
Present options across scope, time, and resources
Promise everything with no plan
Blame teammates publicly in the meeting

questions.explanation: Option triangles give decision makers workable choices.

wrongExplanations.c: False promises create worse conflict later.
wrongExplanations.d: Public blame harms process and trust.

questions.prompt: In salary talks, what should you clarify beyond base pay?

options.text: Nothing; base is the only term
Total compensation elements such as bonus, equity, benefits, and flexibility
Only the office snack budget
Whether you can skip getting terms in writing

questions.explanation: Total comp and related terms often matter as much as base salary.

wrongExplanations.c: Snacks are not the strategic core.

questions.prompt: What should you do after stating an offer?

options.text: Keep talking until you discount yourself
Stop and let silence invite a response
Immediately reveal your reservation point
Apologize for asking

questions.explanation: Silence is a tool; nervous fillers negotiate against yourself.

wrongExplanations.a: Filling air often lowers your own terms.
wrongExplanations.d: Clear asks do not require apology theater.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Ethics, Emotion, and Professional Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on ethics, hardball responses, confirmation, and practice habits.

options.text: Lie about alternatives and authority when useful
Stay competitive without fabricating facts or hiding critical safety risks
Exploit every information gap in ways your profession would condemn
Never put agreements in writing

questions.explanation: Competitive does not mean dishonest; reputation is long-term BATNA.

wrongExplanations.c: Predatory exploitation is rejected in the lesson.

questions.prompt: How can you respond to an aggressive anchor?

options.text: Negotiate against yourself in shock immediately
Pause, re-anchor with rationale, or explicitly reject the frame
Accept it to be polite
Ignore preparation and improvise insults

questions.prompt: What does rapport do in negotiation?

options.text: It requires you to concede every term
It can improve information flow without replacing term clarity
It makes BATNA irrelevant forever
It means never saying no

questions.explanation: Warmth and firmness can coexist; niceness is not compliance.

wrongExplanations.d: Clear nos with options are professional.

options.text: To create “I thought we said…” disputes on purpose
To make terms explicit and reduce misremembered deals
Because oral deals are always more precise
Only when you distrust everyone including yourself about snacks

questions.explanation: Written confirmations turn conversation into operable terms.

wrongExplanations.c: Memory and chat dust are fragile.
wrongExplanations.d: Confirmation is standard for meaningful terms.

questions.prompt: What is a useful freelance negotiation practice?

options.text: Leave revisions, payment, and scope undefined
Define deliverables, timelines, payment schedule, and change-order impacts
Start work with no deposit on risky new clients as a rule
Accept every client regardless of misalignment

questions.explanation: Ambiguity becomes unpaid work; clear SOWs protect both sides.

wrongExplanations.d: Walking away can be the right BATNA.

questions.prompt: Which standard captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: Negotiate so both the terms and the relationship can survive the meeting
Win every point even by lying
Avoid all asks to stay comfortable
Accept first offers by reflex

questions.explanation: Firm, fair, prepared negotiation balances outcomes and relationships.

wrongExplanations.d: First-offer reflex is a listed mistake.
